plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: The machine notes and the honest list of what this computer doesn't have. Knowing exactly which browsers, stand-ins and tools exist let me test the risky parts for real (single-file boot on file://, the hub harness on WebGPU) instead of guessing, so the plan could hand builders proven recipes. I also liked the creative freedom on genre and perspective, set against very firm rules on UX, audio and attract mode. And the source itself: its deadpan tone gave the whole game its voice.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: Three things. First, 'multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own': the hub protocol only applies inside a session, and its README says the game is unaffected outside one, so I couldn't tell whether 'on its own' means it must still run solo or must have its own multiplayer. I chose local couch play on one screen plus solo, and wrote that reading into the plan. Second, the machine notes list three WebGPU flags, but with only those three renderer.capture() failed with a mapAsync error; the kit's check.mjs uses five, and those work. Third, 'prefer file://' next to the kit's own 'ES modules don't load from file://'. Inlining the bundle resolves it, but I had to test that. A smaller one: I wasn't sure whether 'TASK.md's file and folder names' includes the exit-interview file, so I left that name out too.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: Replacing the source's defining input. The original is your body on a board, and a stick mapped straight to position would just be holding still, which isn't a game. It took a physics model and a Monte Carlo search with delayed, human-like bots to find numbers that separate idle, average and expert play on stick, keys and mouse, and I still can't feel the result with hands, so builders must treat those numbers as a strong start, not proof of feel. The other hard part was staying inspired without recreating: keeping the daily judgement, the talking device and the calm instructor while making every character, place and name new. Sizing the plan was also a guess, because I don't know the builder's model or budget.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: Say plainly what multiplayer 'on its own' requires. Put the kit's five working WebGPU flags in the machine notes. Tell the planner which models and effort levels will build from the plan, or give a target length, because a plan sized for a top model may overwhelm a smaller one; I added a cut order to hedge. Mention that the engine's default music volume is 60% and its example songs are quiet, so 'music at 10%' is near silence unless songs are written louder. And in the planner stage, say explicitly whether scratch files may stay in the folder, and whether prototypes are welcome: my spikes were the most valuable thing I did, and I only assumed they were allowed.
